stops.name: Buenos Aires, Fervor de Buenos Aires
stops.campa: At his father's expense, three hundred unnumbered copies of Fervor de Buenos Aires come off the press of the Imprenta Serantes, his sister Norah's woodcut on the cover, no price on the wrapper: Borges and his friends leave copies in overcoat pockets at the Sur cafés and slide them under the doors of people whose opinion he wants. The city of low roofs, cemeteries, and long red sunsets is set down for the first time in the plain, exact free verse he has carried back from Europe. He sails for Europe again within a week of the printing, leaving Buenos Aires a book it did not know it needed.

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Ocampo — the founding of Sur
stops.campa: Victoria Ocampo launches Sur from her house in San Isidro, a review meant to open Argentina onto world letters and the world onto Argentina — Ortega y Gasset, Waldo Frank, and Drieu la Rochelle among its early advisory names. Borges joins the circle from its first issues, translating Woolf and Kafka for its pages, publishing there the essays and fictions that will define him. It is not yet the house where he will meet the friend of his life, but it is already the room, the review, and the patroness that will make that meeting, and most of what follows, possible.

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Ocampo — meeting Bioy Casares
stops.campa: At a lunch in Victoria Ocampo's house Borges meets Adolfo Bioy Casares, seventeen years younger, tall, elegant, already a published novelist: the two withdraw from the other guests to talk and are scolded by their hostess for the rudeness, which only cements the friendship on the spot, and they leave together for the city. From this afternoon grows a partnership of four decades — joint pseudonyms, joint detective stories, a joint anthology of fantastic literature — and the friend to whom, more than any other, Borges will read a new page before anyone else sees it.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "Una vindicación de la Cábala"
stops.campa: In the essay collection Discusión, Borges takes up the hermeneutic machinery of the Kabbalists he first heard named at the Café Colonial: he does not defend their doctrine of a text with no arbitrary syllable, every letter charged and countable, but the cryptographic method itself, which he calls among the strictest and most fantastic literary criticism ever practiced. He names Gershom Scholem, whom he has not yet met, as its living authority. Philosophy and theology, he writes, are branches of the literature of the fantastic — a sentence that will govern his fiction for the next thirty years.
stops.quote: No quiero vindicar la doctrina, sino los procedimientos hermenéuticos o criptográficos que a ella conducen.
stops.quote_source: Una vindicación de la Cábala (first published 1931), in Discusión (1932)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "El acercamiento a Almotásim"
stops.campa: Disguised as a review of a novel that does not exist, "El acercamiento a Almotásim" opens Borges's own door onto the Sufi shelf: the review's fictitious plot, a law student's search through the underworld of Bombay for a man he glimpses only by the goodness his presence leaves in others, is confessed in the essay's own closing note to derive from Farid al-Din Attar's Conference of the Birds, in which thirty birds cross seven valleys to find the Simurgh and find, on the summit, that they themselves compose it. The trick of the false review becomes the mold for every fiction he writes for the next decade.

stops.name: Boedo, the Biblioteca Municipal Miguel Cané
stops.campa: Family money thinning after his father's retirement, Borges takes a post cataloguing books at the modest Miguel Cané municipal library in the working-class barrio of Boedo, poorly paid for work no one much wants. The other clerks, he will recall, spend the working day discussing football and boxing in the basement while he finishes an entire day's quota of cataloguing within the first hour and reads or writes fiction in a corner for the rest of it, hidden, he believes, from everyone; only years later does he learn that a fellow clerk had listed him in the telephone directory under a false name, ashamed of the association with a poet.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the accident on the stairs
stops.campa: Running up a dark stairway on Christmas Eve, Borges catches his head on the freshly painted edge of an open casement window; the wound seems slight, but within days a fever rises, and for weeks he lies between septicemia and death, hallucinating, and, more than the fever itself, fearing for his own mind — that if he recovers his body he may not recover his intellect. He tests himself by trying to write something wholly unlike anything he has written before, to see if the faculty of invention has survived intact. The story that comes, when he finally can hold a pen, is "Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote."

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "Pierre Menard, autor del Quijote"
stops.campa: Sur publishes, in May, the story Borges wrote to prove to himself that his mind had survived the fever: a French symbolist who sets out not to copy but to independently re-arrive, word for word, at several chapters of Don Quixote, and succeeds, so that identical pages carry different meanings written three centuries apart by different men. It is the first work in what will be called, for want of a better word, Borgesian: fiction disguised as literary criticism, criticism disguised as metaphysics, and behind both the same procedure discovered a few years earlier over the false review of Almotásim.
stops.quote: El texto de Cervantes y el de Menard son verbalmente idénticos, pero el segundo es casi infinitamente más rico.
stops.quote_source: Pierre Menard, autor del Quijote, Sur, May 1939

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius"
stops.campa: Sur prints the story of an encyclopedia entry for a country that does not exist, and of the slow, conspiratorial invasion of the real world by the wholly invented idealist planet of Tlön, whose objects duplicate themselves through grief and whose languages have no nouns, only verbs and clusters of adjectives. Borges signs it with the fiction of an editorial footnote reporting his own authorship, blurring, as the Kabbalists blurred the line between commentary and revelation, the boundary between the essay and the world it describes. Bioy Casares walks on in the opening paragraph, remembering the heresiarch who called mirrors and copulation abominable.
stops.quote: Debo a la conjunción de un espejo y de una enciclopedia el descubrimiento de Uqbar.
stops.quote_source: Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius, Sur, May 1940 (opening sentence)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan
stops.campa: His first book of fiction proper gathers eight stories including "La biblioteca de Babel," the universe imagined as an infinite honeycomb of hexagonal galleries holding every possible book, most of them meaningless, a handful of them the exact catalogue and refutation of all the others; and the title story, a Chinese spy's labyrinth-novel in which time itself forks at every choice into simultaneous, incompatible futures. The book sells poorly and loses that year's National Prize for Literature to a work no one now remembers; a jury member later calls the decision, publicly, an outrage. The forking garden becomes, from this printing on, the single most quoted figure in his name.
stops.quote: El universo (que otros llaman la Biblioteca) se compone de un número indefinido, y tal vez infinito, de galerías hexagonales.
stops.quote_source: La biblioteca de Babel, in El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan (1941)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, "El Aleph"
stops.campa: Sur publishes the story of a point in space, glimpsed on the nineteenth step of a cellar staircase on the fictional Calle Garay, that contains every other point in the universe without superposition or transparency, seen all at once from every angle: the narrator, jealous and grieving over a dead woman named Beatriz, sees in it the whole earth and is undone by the seeing. Borges will later call the device a shameless enough metaphor, and dedicate the story, with real and unrequited feeling, to Estela Canto, for whom he had wanted the world itself as a gift and could offer instead only this one sentence's cosmos.
stops.quote: Vi el populoso mar, vi el alba y la tarde... vi el Aleph, desde todos los puntos, vi en el Aleph la tierra.

stops.name: Boedo, the dismissal from the library
stops.campa: Perón's new government, unamused by a writer who has signed manifestos against fascism and made no secret of his contempt for the regime, has him informed that his post at the Miguel Cané library is abolished — and that a position awaits him instead as inspector of poultry and rabbits in the municipal markets. Borges resigns on the spot rather than accept the humiliation, and tells the story for the rest of his life as the clean, absurd shape of the whole Peronist decade: not imprisonment, not exile, but a small, exact, unforgettable insult, delivered with a bureaucrat's straight face.
